A_target.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be [[Definition:Statement|statements]].
If $
eg q \implies 
eg p$ is proved, then $p \implies q$ holds:
:$\paren {
eg q \implies 
eg p} \vdash \paren {p \implies q}$

B_source.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be [[Definition:Statement|statements]].
Then:
:$\paren {p \implies q} \dashv \vdash \paren {\neg q \implies \neg p}$
That is, a [[Definition:Conditional|conditional]] is equivalent to its [[Definition:Contrapositive Statement|contrapositive]].

validity_conditions: Classical logic: P->Q and ~Q->~P have identical truth tables, so proving either establishes the other.
Requires the law of excluded middle / double-negation; the equivalence is weaker in intuitionistic logic (only one direction is free).
proof_plan:
From the [[Rule of Transposition]]:
:$\paren {p \implies q} \dashv \vdash \paren {\neg q \implies \neg p}$
Assume $\neg q$ as hypothesis and derive $\neg p$.
By the [[Rule of Implication]], this establishes $\neg q \implies \neg p$.

By the [[Rule of Transposition]], $p \implies q$ follows.
{{qed}}
